text: The Pacific Ocean covers about 165 million square kilometres
as_written: The Pacific covers about 165 million square kilometres
source: NOAA National Ocean Service / Encyclopaedia Britannica, Pacific Ocean

text: That area is almost a third of Earth's surface (Earth's total surface is about 510 million square kilometres)
as_written: almost a third of the whole surface of the planet
source: NOAA National Ocean Service; Earth surface area from standard geophysical references

text: The Pacific holds roughly 670 million cubic kilometres of water
as_written: roughly 670 million cubic kilometres of water
source: Charette and Smith 2010, 'The Volume of Earth's Ocean', Oceanography 23(2)

text: That is about half of all ocean water
as_written: about half of all the ocean water on Earth
source: Charette and Smith 2010, Oceanography 23(2)

text: The Pacific's average depth is around four kilometres
as_written: Its average depth is around four kilometres
source: Charette and Smith 2010, Oceanography 23(2); NOAA

text: The Challenger Deep is nearly eleven kilometres deep
as_written: nearly eleven kilometres down
source: NOAA Ocean Exploration, Mariana Trench; Gardner et al. bathymetric surveys

text: Mount Everest is about 8.8 kilometres tall
as_written: about 8.8 kilometres tall
source: 2020 China-Nepal survey, 8,848.86 m

text: Everest's summit would sit more than two kilometres below the surface if placed in the trench (10.9 minus 8.8)
as_written: its summit would still sit more than two kilometres below the old surface
source: Derived from NOAA Challenger Deep depth and the 2020 Everest survey

text: The continental shelf typically ends at a depth of a little over a hundred metres
as_written: typically ends at a depth of a little over a hundred metres
source: NOAA National Ocean Service, continental shelf; Harris et al. 2014, Marine Geology

text: Standard atmosphere pressure about 1.5 times sea-level at 4 km below sea level, a little over 3 times at about 10.9 km below
as_written: about one and a half times what you feel on the beach ... a little over three times
source: International Standard Atmosphere (ICAO / US Standard Atmosphere 1976) barometric formula extrapolated below sea level

text: Filling the lost water's volume with air would draw down roughly a fifth of the atmosphere's mass (rough estimate)
as_written: something like a fifth of the entire atmosphere
source: Back-of-envelope: ISA air density, Charette and Smith 2010 volume, atmospheric mass 5.148e18 kg from Trenberth and Smith 2005, J. Climate

text: Pressure at the old sea level would be roughly three quarters of the former value, similar to about two kilometres altitude
as_written: perhaps three quarters of what it was ... an altitude of around two kilometres
source: Derived from the same estimate and the International Standard Atmosphere

text: Long-wave speed in water is the square root of gravity times depth, about 700 km/h at 4 km depth
as_written: roughly 700 kilometres an hour
source: NOAA Center for Tsunami Research, tsunami speed; shallow-water wave theory

text: The 1960 Chile tsunami reached Japan after about a day
as_written: it reached Japan after about a day
source: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information tsunami event records, 1960 Valdivia

text: The Antarctic Circumpolar Current carries more than 100 million cubic metres per second
as_written: more than 100 million cubic metres of water every second
source: Cunningham, Alderson and King 2003, Journal of Geophysical Research (Drake Passage transport about 134 Sv)

text: Ocean remaining after loss would average roughly 1.8 km deep over the basin area, so sea level falls roughly 1.5 to 2 km (rough estimate)
as_written: roughly half of today's average ... something like one and a half to two kilometres
source: Derived from Charette and Smith 2010 (total ocean volume about 1,335 million km3, mean depth about 3.7 km)

text: Today's mean ocean depth is about 3.7 kilometres
as_written: about 3.7 kilometres
source: Charette and Smith 2010, Oceanography 23(2)

text: About 80 percent of world trade by volume goes by sea
as_written: About 80 percent of world trade by volume travels by sea
source: UNCTAD Review of Maritime Transport

text: During the last ice age sea level was around 120 metres lower
as_written: around 120 metres lower than today
source: Lambeck et al. 2014, PNAS, 'Sea level and global ice volumes from the Last Glacial Maximum to the Holocene'

text: Temperature rises about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre of descent in the standard atmosphere, giving about 40 C at 4 km below and above 80 C at the bottom of the trenches
as_written: about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometre ... around 40 degrees Celsius ... above 80 degrees
source: International Standard Atmosphere lapse rate (ICAO Doc 7488), extrapolated

text: The top few metres of the ocean hold as much heat as the entire atmosphere
as_written: The top few metres of the ocean hold as much heat as the entire atmosphere above it
source: NOAA / Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution

text: Oceans have taken up about 90 percent of the extra heat from greenhouse gases
as_written: about 90 percent of the extra heat
source: IPCC AR6 WG1 Chapter 7; von Schuckmann et al. 2020, Earth System Science Data

text: Oceans supply about 90 percent of evaporated water in the water cycle
as_written: about 90 percent of the water that evaporates
source: US Geological Survey Water Science School, The Water Cycle

text: At least half of the oxygen produced each year comes from the ocean, mostly plankton
as_written: at least half of the oxygen produced each year comes from the ocean
source: NOAA National Ocean Service

text: The net oxygen contribution of the ocean is contested because most is consumed by respiration
as_written: whether it matters for the oxygen you breathe is contested
source: Field et al. 1998, Science; Broecker 'Keeping Global Change Honest'; NOAA

text: The atmosphere holds a very large stock of oxygen relative to annual production
as_written: the atmosphere holds an enormous stock of oxygen already
source: Catling and Kasting 2017, Atmospheric Evolution on Inhabitable and Lifeless Worlds

text: The ocean takes up about a quarter of annual CO2 emissions
as_written: about a quarter of the carbon dioxide we emit each year
source: Global Carbon Project, Global Carbon Budget (Friedlingstein et al.)

text: Hudson Bay land is still rising by roughly a centimetre a year
as_written: roughly a centimetre a year
source: Sella et al. 2007, Geophysical Research Letters; Canadian Geodetic Survey GPS data

text: Isostatic rebound from removing 4 km of water would eventually be on the order of a kilometre (water density about a third of mantle rock; rough estimate)
as_written: something on the order of a kilometre
source: Derived from Airy isostasy using seawater density about 1,030 kg/m3 and mantle density about 3,300 kg/m3; Turcotte and Schubert, Geodynamics

text: Ring of Fire hosts about 75 percent of active volcanoes and about 90 percent of earthquakes
as_written: about 75 percent of the world's active volcanoes and about 90 percent of its earthquakes
source: US Geological Survey, Ring of Fire

text: Volcanic activity appears to have increased after the end of the last ice age (debated)
as_written: Some studies find that volcanic activity increased after the ice melted
source: Huybers and Langmuir 2009, Earth and Planetary Science Letters

text: The Moon recedes at about 3.8 centimetres per year, measured by lunar laser ranging
as_written: about 3.8 centimetres a year
source: NASA Lunar Laser Ranging experiment (Apollo retroreflectors)

text: About 300 million cubic kilometres of water would need to move into the Pacific basin (rough estimate)
as_written: roughly 300 million cubic kilometres of water
source: Derived from Charette and Smith 2010 volumes and the Pacific's share of ocean area

text: At 1 billion cubic metres per second refilling would take about ten years, at a tenth of that about a century
as_written: about ten years ... a century
source: Arithmetic from the 300 million km3 estimate

text: The Messinian Salinity Crisis lasted from about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago
as_written: from about 5.96 to 5.33 million years ago
source: Krijgsman et al. 1999, Nature; CIESM 2008 Messinian Salinity Crisis workshop report

text: Messinian salt deposits are up to about two kilometres thick
as_written: up to two kilometres thick
source: Hsu et al. 1973 (DSDP Leg 13); Lofi et al. 2011 seismic studies

text: The extent of Mediterranean desiccation, with drawdown of 1.5 km or more, is contested
as_written: a kilometre and a half or more ... Others think it was only partly drained
source: CIESM 2008; Garcia-Castellanos and Villaseñor 2011, Nature

text: The Zanclean flood peaked around 100 million cubic metres per second and refilled the basin in months to two years
as_written: around 100 million cubic metres per second ... between a few months and two years
source: Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature 462

text: The Zanclean flood occurred about 5.33 million years ago
as_written: About 5.33 million years ago
source: Garcia-Castellanos et al. 2009, Nature 462

text: The Amazon discharges about 200 thousand cubic metres per second
as_written: about 200 thousand cubic metres per second
source: Molinier et al. 1996; NASA Earth Observatory

text: The Atlantic is widening at roughly two and a half centimetres a year while the Pacific shrinks
as_written: roughly two and a half centimetres a year
source: US Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth

text: The oldest ocean floor is about 180 million years old, largely in the western Pacific
as_written: about 180 million years old
source: Müller et al. 2008, Geochemistry Geophysics Geosystems; NOAA age of oceanic lithosphere

text: Amasia hypothesis: Pacific closes in 50 to 200 million years
as_written: between 50 and 200 million years from now
source: Mitchell, Kilian and Evans 2012, Nature 482

text: Alternative Pangaea Ultima hypothesis in which the Atlantic closes first
as_written: the Atlantic will close first ... Pangaea Ultima
source: Scotese, PALEOMAP Project; Nield 2007 'Supercontinent'

text: The mantle transition zone lies between about 410 and 660 kilometres depth
as_written: between about 410 and 660 kilometres below the surface
source: Standard seismological Earth models (PREM, Dziewonski and Anderson 1981)

text: A Brazilian diamond inclusion of ringwoodite held about 1.5 percent water by weight
as_written: about one and a half percent water by weight
source: Pearson et al. 2014, Nature 507

text: Whether the deep mantle holds several oceans' worth of water is disputed
as_written: could hold several times as much water as all of the oceans combined ... Others suspect it holds far less
source: Pearson et al. 2014, Nature; Schmandt et al. 2014, Science; Bercovici and Karato 2003, Nature
